title: Impact of the ‘Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F’ on R&D claims
description: IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F sets the minimum information a federal R&D tax credit (IRC § 41) refund claim must include to be valid.
summary: IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F sets the minimum information a federal R&D tax credit (IRC § 41) refund claim must include to be valid. For U.S. taxpayers filing amended-return research credit claims, the key takeaway is that claims must identify business components, research activities and total qualified expenses, or the IRS may reject them before any merits review.

body.text: IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F sets the minimum information a federal R&D tax credit (IRC § 41) refund claim must include to be valid. For U.S. taxpayers filing amended-return research credit claims, the key takeaway is that claims must identify business components, research activities and total qualified expenses, or the IRS may reject them before any merits review.
1. What the Memorandum Is and Why It Matters

Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F is IRS Office of Chief Counsel field advice dated September 17, 2021 and released on October 15, 2021 (reference POSTS-104459-20). The IRS announced it the same day in news release IR-2021-203. The memorandum sets out the minimum information a refund claim for the IRC § 41 credit for increasing research activities must contain to count as a valid claim at all. Because it is Chief Counsel field advice, it is not binding precedent and may not be cited as such, but it states the position the IRS applies when it screens amended-return research credit claims, and the IRS has implemented it through its published FAQs and claim-screening procedures.

Analysis: The memorandum's main effect is to move substantiation forward in time. Information that taxpayers once assembled during an audit must now, at least in part, be present when the claim is filed. The practical consequence is that the quality of a research credit refund claim is tested twice: first at the threshold, for whether it is a valid claim at all, and only afterward, if it survives, on the merits of the underlying research.
2. Legal Basis: The Specificity Requirement
2.1 Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1)

The memorandum rests on Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1). That regulation requires a refund claim to set out in detail each ground on which it is made, with facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis of the claim. The statement must be verified by a written declaration made under the penalties of perjury. A claim that does not comply is not treated as a claim for refund or credit for any purpose. This is a long-standing rule of general application to all refund claims; the memorandum does not create a new legal standard but applies the existing one specifically to § 41 claims.
2.2 Case Law Cited in the Memorandum
The memorandum relies on the following authorities.

cells: Taxpayers must give the IRS enough information for an intelligent administrative review of the claim.
Specificity lets the IRS consider and resolve claims administratively instead of litigating vague claims.
Filing the required form alone does not make a claim effective.
Where IRC § 7422 or the regulation is not satisfied, sovereign immunity bars suit.
Specificity is a prerequisite to jurisdiction over a refund suit.
The memorandum cites it for the rule that a refund claim must state its grounds with specificity under the regulation.

body.text: Analysis: Because these cases tie specificity to jurisdiction, a deficient research credit claim is not simply adjusted on audit. It can be rejected before anyone reviews the underlying research. Under IRC § 7422(a), no refund suit may be maintained until a claim has been duly filed with the IRS according to the regulations, so a claim that fails the specificity requirement can also foreclose later litigation on the same credit.
3. The Five Required Items of Information
Under the memorandum, a valid § 41 refund claim must, at a minimum:

items: Identify all business components to which the § 41 research credit claim relates for that year.
For each business component, identify all research activities performed.
For each business component, identify all individuals who performed each research activity.
For each business component, identify all information each individual sought to discover.
Provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year. Form 6765 may be used for this.

body.text: The statute defines a business component as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula or invention that is held for sale, lease or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business (IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)). As discussed in Section 6, the IRS has since stopped requiring items 3 and 4 at filing, effective June 18, 2024.
Analysis: Item 4 requires the taxpayer to state the technical uncertainty being investigated.
4. Further Procedural Rules in the Memorandum
4.1 Volume of Documents Is Not Enough

The memorandum states that a mere volume of documents does not meet the taxpayer's obligation. A taxpayer that submits documents, such as a credit study, must specify the exact pages that support each specific fact. The memorandum adds that the IRS has no affirmative obligation to sort through a taxpayer's records.
4.2 Penalties-of-Perjury Declaration

The memorandum takes the position that the taxpayer's signature on the amended return generally serves as the penalties-of-perjury declaration for the claim and its attachments. It also says that facts submitted later need a new signed declaration, and acknowledges that this view is taken in the absence of direct guidance.
4.3 Statute of Limitations

The memorandum notes that no statutory provision deals specifically with the limitations period for § 41 research credit claims; IRC § 6511 governs. Under § 6511(a), a claim must be filed within 3 years from the time the return was filed or 2 years from the time the tax was paid, whichever expires later.

Analysis: A claim rejected as deficient does not stop the limitations clock. If the § 6511 period has run, the taxpayer may not be able to refile a corrected claim. This makes getting the claim right on first filing especially important, and it is why the perfection opportunity described in Section 5 has practical value: a claim perfected within the IRS's 45-day window is treated as a perfected version of the original filing rather than as a new, potentially late, claim.
5. Implementation: Grace Period, Transition Period and Perfection

cells: The five items are required for timely refund claims. Claims postmarked before this date are not subject to them (IRS FAQ 2).
The window to perfect a deficient claim was set at 45 days, up from the 30 days first announced.
Through Jan. 10, 2024; then 2025; then 2026; now Jan. 10, 2027

body.text: The IRS research credit claims FAQ page (last updated October 1, 2026) now says the transition period was extended through January 10, 2027. IRS updates of October 30, 2023 and November 25, 2024 extended it through January 10, 2025 and January 10, 2026, respectively.

During the transition period, the IRS tells taxpayers that a claim is deficient by Letter 6426C or Letter 6428. The letter names the missing items and gives 45 days to perfect the claim before the IRS makes its final determination. If the missing information is not provided, or is insufficient, the IRS may reject the claim.

Analysis: The transition period has now been extended repeatedly, but each extension has been announced close to the prior expiration date. Taxpayers filing claims near January 10, 2027 should not assume a further extension and should treat the claim as if no perfection opportunity will be available.
6. The June 18, 2024 Change (FAQ 21)

Effective June 18, 2024, the IRS no longer requires research credit refund claims to include item 3 (the names of the individuals who performed each research activity) or item 4 (the information each individual sought to discover). Taxpayers must still provide:

items: the business components to which the credit relates;
the research activities performed for each business component; and
the total qualified wage, supply and contract research expenses for the claim year, which may be reported on Form 6765.

body.text: The IRS may still request the two waived items if the claim is selected for examination.
Note on wording: The IRS FAQ calls it effective June 18, 2024 and does not use the postmark wording.
Analysis: The relief is about timing, not substance. The burden of producing the information is postponed, not removed. So the records behind items 3 and 4 still need to exist and be retrievable.
7. How the Memorandum's Approach Carried Into Form 6765
7.1 Timeline of the Form 6765 Revisions

items: September 15, 2023: The IRS previewed a revised Form 6765 with a new business component section, then labeled Section F.
June 21, 2024 (IR-2024-171): The IRS released a revised draft. The business component section became Section G, its scope was reduced, and it was made optional for all filers for tax year 2024.
October 1, 2025 (IR-2025-99): The IRS made Section G optional for all filers for tax year 2025 and extended the comment period on the draft instructions through March 31, 2026.

Current instructions (Rev. December 2025, for use with the January 2025 revision of Form 6765): Section G is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to the exceptions below.

body.text: Section G is now in force: it applies to tax years beginning after 2025.
7.2 Content of Section G
Under the current instructions, Section G asks for:

items: the EIN of the entity conducting the research and its principal business activity code (49(a)-(b));
the business component's name or unique alphanumeric identifier (49(c));
the component type: Product, Process or All Others (49(d));
the software type, where relevant: IUS, DFS, Non-IUS or Excepted from IUS treatment (49(e));

column 49(f), which currently applies only to amended returns or administrative adjustment requests (AARs) that claim a credit not reported on the original return or that increase the original credit, and is not required for timely original returns, including returns filed on extension; and
QREs by component: wages for direct research, supervision and support; supplies; computer rental or lease costs; and contract research (columns 50-56).

body.text: Analysis: Column 49(f) is the point at which the form most directly reflects the memorandum: it imposes additional information only on refund claims, the category of filing the memorandum addresses.
7.3 The 80% / Top 50 Rule

Filers required to complete Section G must report, in descending order of QREs, the business components that together make up at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 components. The rest are reported together on one line as "Aggregate Business Components," with amounts entered only in columns 50-56. Section G is not required for (i) a qualified small business under § 41(h)(3) that checked the box to claim the reduced payroll tax credit, or (ii) a taxpayer whose controlled-group QREs on line 48 are $1.5 million or less, whose average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are $50 million or less, and who is reporting the credit on an original return. All three conditions in (ii) must be met.

Sampling must follow Rev. Proc. 2011-42. Filing the form does not mean the IRS accepts the sample. The 80%/Top 50 components must be reported whether or not they were sampled, and sampled components must be labeled "sample." The sampling plan must be attached as a file named "Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf."
Hypothetical example (tax year beginning after 2025, original return, taxpayer not eligible for either exception):

Total QREs are $2,000,000, and 80% of that is $1,600,000. The cumulative total first reaches or passes $1,600,000 at component D ($1,700,000, or 85%). So components A-D are reported individually, and E and F ($150,000 each, $300,000 combined) go on the aggregate line. The $1.5 million QRE exception does not apply, because the QREs are $2,000,000.
7.4 Section E Questions

items: the total number of business components generating the line 48 QREs, not just those reported in Section G (line 37);
officers' wages included in QREs (line 38);
whether QREs relate to an acquisition or disposition during the year (line 39); and
whether any new categories of expenses are included, which must also be included and adjusted in the base years (line 40).

body.text: The current instructions confirm controlled-group reporting requirements: the 80%/Top 50 test is generally applied at the controlled group level (members filing separately measure the 80% against their own QREs); all members must file consistently with the designated member's method and election; each member makes its own payroll tax credit election, with the $500,000 amount allocated by share of QREs; and the Item B attachment must list each member's EIN, name, designated-member status, QREs and credit share, along with the number of members in the current and prior years.
8. Interaction With Section 174 and the 174A Correction

If a credit claim fails because it lacks CCM-level substantiation, the taxpayer loses the credit, but the costs must still be capitalized and amortized under § 174: over 5 years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research.

That description reflects § 174 as amended by the TCJA, which applied to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021. Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025, added IRC § 174A. Under § 174A, domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 are deductible currently, and software development costs are treated as research or experimental expenditures. A taxpayer may instead elect to capitalize them and amortize them over a period of not less than 60 months, beginning when the taxpayer first realizes benefits. Foreign research expenditures remain under § 174, with 15-year amortization. Transition rules in Pub. L. 119-21 also allow certain unamortized domestic amounts from 2022-2024 to be deducted. Eligible small businesses (those meeting the § 448(c) gross receipts test for their first tax year beginning after 2024) could elect to apply § 174A retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021; that election had to be made within one year of the July 4, 2025 enactment date, and required amended returns for each affected year.

Analysis: For domestic research in tax years beginning after 2024, the capitalization half of the "dual penalty" largely no longer applies. It remains relevant to foreign research and to domestic expenditures from 2022-2024 that were capitalized and not recovered through a transition election. Because the small business retroactive election window closed in July 2026, an eligible taxpayer that did not make it cannot now use that route. The credit-loss half is unchanged: a claim that fails the memorandum's standard still loses the credit. The § 174A elections also interact with refund claims in practice, because amended returns filed to implement § 174A changes may be the same returns on which a taxpayer claims or increases a research credit, and those claims must meet the memorandum's requirements.
9. Context for the Credit at Stake

items: Alternative simplified credit (IRC § 41(c)(4)): 14% of QREs above 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding years. If there were no QREs in any one of those three years, the credit is 6% of current-year QREs. In practice, a taxpayer that starts research and claims every year gets the 6% rate until it has three prior years of QREs.

Payroll tax election for qualified small businesses (IRC § 41(h)): A qualified small business has gross receipts under $5,000,000 and no gross receipts for any year before the 5-taxable-year period ending with the current year. The election amount is capped at $250,000, increased by $250,000 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022 (so $500,000 in total). An election cannot be made after elections in 5 or more preceding years.

body.text: Analysis: The memorandum, FAQ 21 and Section G all reward records that are organized by business component and created at the time the research is done. A documentation system that already captures components, activities, personnel, uncertainties and QREs by category can produce both the three items still required at filing and the two items the IRS may request on examination, and it can also populate the Section G component listing now required for tax years beginning after 2025.
